title: Combination Sum Problem

constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, serialized as [candidates,target].
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialized 2D integer array containing the unique combinations.

content.problemStatement:
You receive an array of **distinct** integers `candidates` and a target integer `target`, output *a list of all **unique combinations** of* `candidates` *where the chosen numbers sum to* `target`*.* You may output the combinations in **any order**.

The **same** number may be chosen from `candidates` an **unlimited number of times**. Two combinations are unique if the frequency of no fewer than one of the chosen numbers is different.

The test cases are generated such that the number of unique combinations that sum up to `target` is less than `150` combinations for the given input.

notes: Candidates are distinct and positive, so sorting enables safe pruning when a candidate exceeds the remaining target.
solution.approach: Sort the candidates and use depth-first backtracking. At each recursion level, choose candidates from the current index onward so combinations remain nondecreasing and permutations are not duplicated. Reuse the same index to allow unlimited selections. Stop a branch when the remaining sum becomes smaller than the next candidate.

optimal.complexity: Output-sensitive exponential time and O(T/minCandidate) auxiliary recursion space.
optimal.description: Backtrack over candidate indices in nondecreasing order. Reusing the current index permits unlimited use, while advancing indices prevents permutation duplicates.

bruteForce.description: Enumerate sequences of candidate choices up to the target depth, then deduplicate permutations.

solution.timeComplexity: Output-sensitive exponential; O(N^(T/minCandidate)) in the worst case, excluding output size.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(T/minCandidate) recursion and path space, excluding the returned combinations.

followUps: How would the algorithm change if each candidate could be used at most once?
How would you count the combinations without constructing every combination?

learningObjectives: Use recursive backtracking with a mutable path.
Prevent duplicate combinations by maintaining nondecreasing choice order.
Apply pruning using sorted positive candidates.
